lead: Network devices move frames or packets from one end of a network to another. Different devices use different logic to decide where to send the data. Hubs repeat electrical signals, switches learn MAC addresses, bridges filter traffic between segments, and routers forward IP packets based on routing tables. These devices appear in home Wi‑Fi routers, office Ethernet closets, campus backbones and ISP core networks.
prereq: You need: basic data communication concepts from Chapter 1.1.

blocks.text: A hub operates at the physical layer. It receives a voltage signal on one port, amplifies it, and sends the same signal out on all other ports.
Because the hub does not examine any header fields, every attached device shares one collision domain. If two devices transmit simultaneously, a collision occurs and both frames are corrupted.

items: Simple and cheap, often used in small home networks before switches became inexpensive.
Creates a single broadcast domain and a single collision domain.

blocks.where: Signal_out is the amplified voltage; Gain is the amplification factor; Signal_in is the received voltage.

sections.h3: Switch – MAC‑address learning at the data‑link layer

blocks.text: A switch works at layer 2. Each port belongs to a separate collision domain but all ports share one broadcast domain.
When a frame arrives, the switch reads the source MAC address and stores it in a MAC table together with the incoming port.

items: Read destination MAC address from the frame header.
Look up the destination in the MAC table.
If an entry exists, forward the frame only to the associated port.
If no entry exists, flood the frame to all ports except the source.
Reduces collisions compared to a hub.
Supports full‑duplex links, allowing simultaneous send and receive.

sections.h3: Bridge and Router – segment filtering and IP routing

blocks.text: A bridge is a two‑port switch. It separates two Ethernet segments and forwards frames only when the destination MAC belongs to the opposite segment.
A router works at layer 3. It receives an IP packet, checks the destination IP address, and looks up the best next‑hop in a routing table.

items: Extract destination IP from the packet header.
Match the IP against routing table prefixes.
Encapsulate the packet in a new frame with the next‑hop MAC address and send it out the chosen interface.
Creates separate broadcast domains, reducing unnecessary traffic.
Implements NAT, firewall rules and QoS in many ISP routers.

blocks.where: PrefixLength(r) is the number of bits in the prefix; IP is the destination address; Prefix(r) is the network prefix of route r.

figure.caption: Data moves from a source through a hub, a switch, a bridge and finally a router before reaching the destination.

spec.aria: Block diagram shows data moving through a hub, switch, bridge and router from source to destination.

examples.question: Host A wants to send a 1 MB file to Host D over a 100 Mbps switched LAN. Compute the transmission time assuming negligible switching delay.
steps: Convert file size to bits: 1 MB = 1 × 8 Mbits = 8 Mbits.
Use the formula Transmission time = File size (bits) ÷ Link speed (bits/s).
examples.check:
size_mb = 1
bits = size_mb * 8 * 10**6
speed_mbps = 100
time_s = bits / (speed_mbps * 10**6)
print(round(time_s, 2))

traps: Assuming a hub creates separate collision domains for each port; it actually creates a single collision domain.
Treating a switch as a router and expecting it to examine IP addresses; a basic switch only looks at MAC addresses.
Adding the hub’s amplification gain to the transmission time calculation; amplification does not affect data size or speed.
Thinking that a bridge can route between different IP subnets; a bridge works only at layer 2 and cannot forward IP packets across subnets.

quiz.q: What layer of the OSI model does a hub operate in?
Explain why a switch reduces collisions compared to a hub.
quiz.a: Each switch port forms its own collision domain, so only devices sharing the same port can collide. The hub shares one collision domain across all ports, causing collisions when any two devices transmit simultaneously.

quiz.q: A frame arrives at a switch with destination MAC address not present in the MAC table. What does the switch do?
quiz.a: The switch floods the frame out all ports except the one it arrived on.

quiz.q: Given a routing table entry 192.168.10.0/24 → Interface 2, what next‑hop does a router choose for a packet destined to 192.168.10.45?
quiz.a: The packet matches the 192.168.10.0/24 prefix, so the router forwards it out Interface 2.

quiz.q: In a campus network, a bridge connects two Ethernet segments. If a broadcast frame is sent on Segment A, which segments will receive it?
quiz.a: Both Segment A and Segment B will receive the broadcast because bridges forward broadcast frames to all ports except the source port.

quiz.q: Compare the broadcast domains created by a hub, a switch, and a router.
quiz.a: A hub and a switch each create a single broadcast domain for all attached ports. A router separates broadcast domains; each router interface defines its own broadcast domain, preventing broadcasts from crossing interfaces.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern data centers replace traditional switches with software‑defined networking (SDN) controllers that program flow tables dynamically. Research on programmable data planes uses P4 language to define custom packet processing beyond MAC‑address lookup. Emerging IoT gateways combine bridge and router functions with protocol translation. For deeper study, search for "OpenFlow" and "segment routing" in recent networking literature.
